title: How to Start Family Worship in Five Minutes
excerpt: Family worship is not a production. It is a few honest minutes around a table, repeated until it becomes the air your children breathe.
body:
Most parents who want family worship never start it, and the reason is almost always the same. They are waiting to feel ready, to find the right book, to have a house calm enough to pull it off. That day does not come. Your children grow up in the house you actually have, not the one you keep meaning to build. So start small enough that you cannot fail.

## Why five minutes is the right size

Family worship has a long history, and almost none of it looks like a polished thirty-minute lesson. The Puritans called it the duty of the household, and what they meant was simple: a father or mother gathering the people under their roof to read a little Scripture, pray, and sing. Deuteronomy 6 tells parents to talk of God's commands "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise." That is not a curriculum. It is a rhythm woven through an ordinary day.

Five minutes works because you will actually do it. A practice you keep beats a practice you admire. I have abandoned more ambitious plans than I can count. The nights we simply read three verses and prayed are the nights my sons remember.

## The three movements

Keep it to three things. Read, talk, pray.

**Read.** Pick one short passage. A psalm, a few verses from the Gospel you are walking through, a proverb. Read it aloud. Do not explain everything. Let the words sit.

**Talk.** Ask one question. Not a quiz. "What do you think God is like in this verse?" or "What is hard to believe here?" Let a child's strange answer stand without correcting it into the ground. You are training them to bring their real thoughts to Scripture, not to perform the right ones.

**Pray.** Short prayers, out loud, by name. Pray for the math test. Pray for the grandmother in the hospital. Let the children pray too, even when it is one mumbled sentence. They are learning that God is spoken to, not just spoken about.

## Pick a time you already own

Do not invent a new slot in the day. Attach worship to something that already happens. Dinner is the obvious one, because everyone is already sitting and trapped. Bedtime works for younger children. Breakfast works if your mornings are not a war.

The anchor matters more than the hour. If you try to do it whenever there is a gap, there will never be a gap. Choose the meal or the moment, and let the consistency carry you on the nights you have nothing left.

## Expect it to go badly

It will. Someone will be in a mood. A toddler will throw a fork during the prayer. A teenager will sigh like you have asked for blood. You will feel like a fraud reading about grace through clenched teeth.

Keep going anyway. The point was never a perfect five minutes. The point is that your children grow up knowing this family stops, opens the Bible, and talks to God. That memory forms slowly, under the surface, through a hundred mediocre evenings. You are not staging a moment. You are laying down a riverbed.

Resist the urge to lecture. The temptation in family worship is to turn five minutes into a sermon because you finally have a captive audience. Do not. Read, ask, pray, release them. A short practice they do not dread will outlast a long one they endure.

## This week

Pick the meal. Tonight or tomorrow, before anyone leaves the table, read one psalm, ask one question, and pray for one thing by name. Do not announce a new program. Just do it, and do it again the next night. Give it two weeks before you judge whether it is working. By then it will have started to belong to you.

If you want a structure to lean on, the family devotions and catechism resources at /family/devotions and /family/catechism give you the words for the nights you have none. But the words are not the point. The showing up is the point. Start with five minutes you can keep.
